finalArgument.thesis: Biblical reliability remains underdetermined when theological guarantees, flexible oral transmission, literary development, and harmonization can each conceal uncertainty within the surviving record.
premises: Permitting miracles does not make particular reports historically probable when divine causation supplies no independently traceable signature for disciplined assessment.

newArguments.title: Eyewitness control needs a denominator
newArguments.text: Successful correction anecdotes need a denominator: how many reports reached identifiable witnesses, how often challenges were preserved, and what occurred beyond their authority? Without those quantities, proximity is reassuring possibility rather than measured control. Mapping circulation, rival receptions, and correction episodes could produce bounded confidence instead of assuming either perfect policing or unrestricted invention.

newArguments.title: Transmission tests can disagree
newArguments.text: External stability and internal unity answer different questions. Unanimous late witnesses show that a passage stabilized before their recoverable ancestry, while contextual seams may suggest earlier composition. Neither test erases the other. Rational judgment combines them: external evidence penalizes late interpolation, internal evidence may sustain early redaction, and confidence depends on a dated model explaining both seam and attestation.

newArguments.title: Two ledgers for value and origin
newArguments.text: A later saying may remain ethically profound while losing force as testimony from Jesus; authentic origin likewise cannot guarantee moral authority. Each passage therefore needs separate ledgers for historical provenance and philosophical or literary merit. This prevents canon from deciding history and prevents textual criticism from masquerading as a verdict on whether a teaching is wise, humane, or spiritually fruitful.
